questions.question: What are the two ways to create a thread in Java?
questions.title: Two Ways to Create Threads in Java
questions.direct_answer: You can create a thread by **extending the Thread class** and overriding `run()`, or by **implementing the Runnable interface** and passing it to a Thread constructor. A third modern approach is implementing **Callable** for tasks that return a value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core multithreading knowledge — creating threads is the starting point
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that calling run() directly does not create a new thread — you must call start()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Immediately mention which approach is preferred (Runnable) and why

sections.title: Both Approaches
Key Points
sections.content:
- Both require overriding the run() method
- Always call start(), not run() — calling run() directly executes in the current thread
- start() creates a new OS thread and calls run() on it
- Runnable is preferred (explained in thread-vs-runnable topic)
- Lambda is the cleanest syntax for short tasks
- Callable is used when the thread needs to return a value or throw checked exceptions

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: There are two classic ways to create a thread in Java. First, extend the Thread class and override the run() method. Second, implement the Runnable interface and pass your Runnable to a Thread constructor. In both cases, you must call start() on the Thread object — not run(). Calling run() directly just executes the code in your current thread, no new thread is created. In modern Java, Runnable is almost always preferred over extending Thread, and with Java 8 lambdas, you can just write new Thread(() -> doSomething()).start() without any class at all.

followup_questions: What happens if you call run() instead of start()?
Why is implementing Runnable preferred over extending Thread?
What is Callable and how is it different from Runnable?

groups.heading: Extending Thread
groups.text: You extend the Thread class and override run(). Simple, but burns your one shot at inheritance and couples your task to the threading mechanism. You call start() to launch it.

groups.heading: Implementing Runnable
groups.text: You implement Runnable and pass it to a Thread constructor. The task and the thread are separate. Same Runnable can run in a new Thread, an ExecutorService, or even synchronously — without changing the task class.

items: Prefer Runnable (or a lambda) for all application tasks — it works with thread pools and is better OOP design.
Extending Thread is only justified in framework code where you need to modify Thread's own behavior.

beats.text: In your order app: new Thread(() -> processOrder(order)).start() creates a one-off thread with a lambda. Or submit the same lambda to an ExecutorService thread pool — same task, no code change.

speakable_v2.cap: Always call start(), never run() — and prefer Runnable over extending Thread in almost every real project.

questions.question: What happens if you call run() instead of start() on a Thread?
questions.title: run() vs start() on a Thread Object
questions.direct_answer: Calling `run()` directly executes the code **in the current thread** — no new thread is created. The method behaves like any regular method call. Only `start()` creates a new OS thread and schedules the `run()` method to execute in that new thread.

interviewer_intent.testing: Very commonly asked — many freshers get this wrong in coding exercises
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling run() and wondering why threads aren't concurrent
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what start() actually does internally — calls the native thread creation mechanism

sections.title: run() vs start() Behavior
What start() Does
sections.content:
When you call `thread.start()`:
1. A new OS thread is created (native system call)
2. The new thread is placed in the **RUNNABLE** state
3. The JVM schedules the new thread to execute `run()`
4. `start()` returns immediately in the calling thread — it doesn't wait

When you call `thread.run()` directly:
- No new thread is created
- `run()` executes synchronously in the calling thread
- It's just a regular method call

Calling `start()` twice on the same Thread throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: If you call run() directly, no new thread is created. The code in run() just executes in your current thread, exactly like calling any regular method. You'd see Thread.currentThread().getName() returning 'main' instead of 'Thread-0'. To actually create a new thread and run the code concurrently, you must call start(). start() does the heavy lifting — it makes a system call to create an actual OS thread, puts it in the runnable state, and then returns immediately. The JVM scheduler will then run your run() method in that new thread at some point. And if you call start() twice on the same thread, you get an IllegalThreadStateException.

followup_questions: Can you call start() more than once on a Thread?
In what state does a thread enter when start() is called?

questions.question: How do you create a thread using a lambda expression in Java 8?
questions.title: Creating Threads with Lambda Expressions
questions.direct_answer: Since `Runnable` is a **functional interface**, you can use a **lambda expression** directly as the `Runnable` argument to the Thread constructor. This is the most concise way to create a thread for short inline tasks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern Java thread creation syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Runnable is a functional interface — thinking lambdas only work with Stream API
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention anonymous Runnable class vs lambda vs method reference — all three work

sections.title: Thread Creation Syntax Evolution
Key Points
sections.content:
- Runnable has one abstract method: void run() — so it's a functional interface
- Lambda syntax: () -> { body } or () -> expression for single statements
- Method references work too: ClassName::methodName
- Lambdas are cleaner but equivalent to anonymous Runnable class
- For production code with many threads, prefer ExecutorService over raw Thread

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Since Runnable is a functional interface — it has just one abstract method, run() — you can use a lambda expression wherever a Runnable is expected. So instead of the old anonymous class syntax, you just write new Thread(() -> yourCode()).start(). This is much cleaner and is the standard way to write quick thread creation in Java 8 and beyond. For more complex scenarios in production, you'd typically use an ExecutorService with a thread pool rather than creating raw Thread objects — but the lambda syntax applies there too.

followup_questions: Why can a Runnable be replaced by a lambda?

beats.text: Since Java 8, any interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface and can be implemented with a lambda. Runnable has exactly one abstract method — run(), which takes no arguments and returns void. So any lambda that matches that shape is automatically a valid Runnable.
Before Java 8, creating a Runnable meant writing an anonymous class with boilerplate. Lambdas eliminated that overhead, making thread creation in Java clean and readable.

items: Lambda: new Thread(() -> processOrder()).start() — the lambda IS the Runnable.
Method reference: new Thread(OrderService::processNext).start() — method reference as Runnable.
Named Runnable: Runnable task = () -> processOrder(); — assign and reuse anywhere.

beats.text: non-obvious: The lambda captures variables from the enclosing scope, but only if they're effectively final. If you try to capture a loop variable that changes, the compiler will refuse. This trips up freshers who want to pass a counter into a thread lambda.

items: Lambda syntax is great for short tasks — for complex multi-step logic, a named class is more readable.
Raw Thread creation is fine for learning, but production code should use ExecutorService with thread pools.

speakable_v2.cap: Lambdas make Runnable creation almost invisible — but remember to use an ExecutorService in real applications.

questions.question: What is Callable and how does it differ from Runnable?
questions.title: Callable vs Runnable in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Callable** is like Runnable but its `call()` method **returns a value** and can **throw checked exceptions**. It's used with `ExecutorService.submit()` which returns a `Future` — letting you retrieve the result later.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to get results from thread execution
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about Future or how to get the Callable result
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the ExecutorService.submit() and Future.get() pattern

sections.title: Runnable vs Callable
sections.content:
| Aspect | Runnable | Callable<V> |
|---|---|---|
| Method | run() | call() |
| Return type | void | V (generic) |
| Throws checked? | No | Yes |
| Used with | Thread, Executor | ExecutorService.submit() |
| Returns | Nothing | Future<V> |
| Available since | Java 1 | Java 5 |

sections.title: Callable with Future
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Callable is like Runnable but it returns a value and can throw checked exceptions. With Runnable, your run() method returns void — there's no way to get a result back. With Callable, you call() method returns a generic type. You submit a Callable to an ExecutorService and get back a Future object. The Future is like a promise — you can call future.get() to block and wait for the result, or check if it's done with isDone(). The other advantage over Runnable is that Callable.call() can throw checked exceptions, so you don't need to wrap them in RuntimeException.

speakable_v2.hook: Runnable is fire-and-forget — Callable lets you get a result back from the thread, which is what you need most of the time in real work.

groups.heading: Runnable
groups.text: Has run() which returns void and can't throw checked exceptions. Perfect for tasks where you don't need a result back — fire off the work and move on. Works with Thread or ExecutorService.

groups.heading: Callable<V>
groups.text: Has call() which returns a typed value V and can throw checked exceptions. Submit it to an ExecutorService and you get a Future<V> back. Call future.get() when you need the result — it blocks until the task completes.

items: Use Runnable for background work where you don't care about the result — logging, sending emails.
Use Callable when you need the computed result back — price calculation, external API call, file parsing.

beats.text: In your order app: submit a Callable that calls an external shipping API and returns a shipping cost. Do other work while it runs. Then call future.get() to get the cost and complete the order total.

speakable_v2.cap: If your background task produces a value you need, Callable with Future is the pattern — don't force a result back through shared state.

questions.question: What is an ExecutorService and why is it preferred over creating threads directly?
questions.title: ExecutorService vs Raw Thread Creation
questions.direct_answer: **ExecutorService** manages a **thread pool**, reusing threads instead of creating and destroying them for each task. This avoids the overhead of OS thread creation, controls concurrency, and provides lifecycle management — making it the standard approach in production Java code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the production approach to thread management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating new Thread() for every task in production code — doesn't scale
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the common Executors factory methods: newFixedThreadPool, newCachedThreadPool, newSingleThreadExecutor

sections.title: ExecutorService Usage
Key Points
sections.content:
- Thread creation is expensive — reusing threads is much more efficient
- ExecutorService separates task definition from thread management
- Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) — fixed N threads, tasks queue if all busy
- Executors.newCachedThreadPool() — creates new threads as needed, reuses idle ones
- Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() — single thread, tasks execute sequentially
- Always shutdown() after use to release thread resources
- Spring Boot uses an internal ExecutorService for handling HTTP requests

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Creating a new Thread for every task is expensive because each Thread maps to an OS thread, which involves a system call and memory allocation. If you create a new thread for every HTTP request and have 1000 concurrent requests, you'd create 1000 threads — which wastes memory and causes excessive context switching. ExecutorService solves this with a thread pool: you create a fixed number of threads upfront, and tasks queue up to be executed by those threads. Threads are reused across tasks. The common factory methods are newFixedThreadPool for a bounded pool, newCachedThreadPool for elastic workloads, and newSingleThreadExecutor for sequential task processing.

followup_questions: What happens to tasks when an ExecutorService is shut down?
What is the difference between shutdown() and shutdownNow()?
How does Spring Boot's @Async relate to ExecutorService?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app processing order requests with multiple threads
familiarity_anchors: a pool of taxi drivers waiting for fares vs hiring a new driver for every trip
a team of customer service reps vs firing and hiring for each call
a thread pool at a call center
speakable_v2.hook: Creating a new Thread for every task is like hiring a new employee for every order — by the time they're onboarded, the work is almost done.

beats.text: ExecutorService is a thread pool manager. You create a fixed or variable number of threads upfront, then submit tasks to it. Threads are reused across tasks instead of being created and destroyed for each one. This saves the cost of OS thread creation and controls concurrency.

Creating an OS thread is expensive — it involves system calls and memory allocation. If your order app creates a new Thread for every incoming request, 1000 concurrent requests mean 1000 thread-creation operations plus context switching overhead. A thread pool avoids all of that.

items: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n): exactly n threads, tasks queue when all are busy.
Executors.newCachedThreadPool(): creates new threads as needed, reuses idle ones — good for short-lived tasks.
Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(): one thread, tasks run sequentially — good for ordered processing.

beats.text: production trap: Always call shutdown() on the ExecutorService when you're done. If you don't, the pool threads keep running as non-daemon threads and the JVM won't exit even after your main logic finishes.

items: Forgetting shutdown() keeps the JVM alive indefinitely — a common memory and process leak.
An unbounded cached thread pool under very high load can create thousands of threads and exhaust memory.

speakable_v2.cap: ExecutorService is the production way to manage threads — raw Thread creation is for learning, not for shipping code.

questions.question: What is a daemon thread in Java and when would you use one?
questions.title: Daemon Threads in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **daemon thread** is a background thread that is automatically killed when all non-daemon (user) threads finish. Set with `thread.setDaemon(true)` before `start()`. Use for background services like logging, cleanup, or monitoring that should not prevent JVM shutdown.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JVM shutdown behavior and thread lifecycle
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting daemon after start() — throws IllegalThreadStateException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete use case: monitoring thread that polls health metrics should be daemon

sections.title: Daemon Thread Example
Key Points
sections.content:
- setDaemon(true) must be called BEFORE start() — else IllegalThreadStateException
- JVM exits when all non-daemon threads finish, regardless of running daemon threads
- Daemon threads do NOT get a finally block executed on JVM shutdown
- The JVM's GC thread is a daemon thread
- Use case: background polling, log flushing, cache cleanup
- Don't use daemon threads for critical work that must complete on shutdown

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: A daemon thread is a background thread that the JVM automatically kills when all user threads finish. You set it with thread.setDaemon(true) — and this must be called before start(), otherwise you get an IllegalThreadStateException. The typical use case is background services: a monitoring thread that periodically checks system health, a cache eviction thread, or a log flusher. These are services you want running while the application is up, but you don't want them to prevent the application from shutting down. The JVM's garbage collector itself runs as a daemon thread.

speakable_v2.hook: Daemon threads are the JVM's background helpers — they run silently and get killed automatically when the real work is done.

beats.text: A daemon thread is a background thread that the JVM automatically terminates when all non-daemon (user) threads finish. Set with thread.setDaemon(true) before calling start(). If you call it after start(), you get an IllegalThreadStateException.

Some services should run only while the application is alive but shouldn't prevent it from shutting down. A health-check poller, a cache cleanup job, or a log flusher — these shouldn't keep the JVM hanging after all real work is done.

items: User threads (non-daemon): keep the JVM alive until they complete — all threads by default.
Daemon threads: automatically killed when all user threads finish — GC runs as one.

beats.text: sharp edge: Daemon threads don't get finally blocks executed on JVM shutdown. If your daemon thread has open file handles or database connections in a finally block, those won't close. Don't put critical cleanup in a daemon thread — use a JVM shutdown hook instead.

items: Never use daemon threads for work that must complete — like writing a final record to a database.
setDaemon(true) must be called before start() — otherwise it throws IllegalThreadStateException.

speakable_v2.cap: Daemon threads are for background services that should vanish quietly when the app exits — not for anything that must finish.
